meta.what: Every FAILING judge rubric justification (>=120 chars, deduped) this campaign has produced.
meta.why: The negative population for the repeat-objection comparator (WP-647). Two objections from DIFFERENT run families are never the same objection, so every cross-family pair is a labelled negative the delivery cannot enumerate or hand-fit.

rows.justification: Although the new command correctly prefers per-task files when present, it explicitly falls back to synthesizing TaskResult records from an existing aggregate summary, and also accepts an aggregate summary file as the sole results input. That conflicts with the overall requirement that stored per-task files are the evidence and the aggregate under suspicion must not be trusted as input. It also reconstructs requirement identities and satisfaction positions rather than preserving actual per-requirement evidence.

The ledger is placed appropriately, but the evidence design is incomplete: the diff adds a probe.json allow-rule without committing any probe.json files, and the judge confirmed zero such tracked artifacts. The render-site strategy is coherent and preserves the single accumulator and raw suite evidence, but renderCompletionReviewConcerns does not actually guarantee its documented strict character budget for arbitrary inputs. A single concern is returned intact without any length check, and the overflow path always returns the oldest and newest entries intact even when those entries alone exceed maxChars. Because the function accepts unrestricted strings, the completion-review rendering remains unbounded for those cases, contrary to the overall requirement that no rendered evidence-path string be unbounded.

Although the design passes the named fixtures and bounds reads, it does not reliably preserve original bytes or report every unpreserved corruption. Preserved files are converted from Buffer to UTF-8 strings and later written as strings, which can corrupt non-UTF-8 ignored files. More seriously, the added unit test confirms deletion of an unpreserved ignored file produces no restore entry, so applyCleanupPlan neither restores nor warns about it. For modified unpreserved files, reporting is only console.warn and is not added to the batch CheckRun output. Thus budget-exceeded corruption can still be silently passed off by the batch, contrary to the overall goal.

The diff contains concrete goal-breaking defects. Preserved ignored-file bytes are converted from Buffer to UTF-8 text and restored with writeFile(string), so non-UTF-8 files are not byte-preserved. For an ignored file excluded by the preservation budget and then deleted, the committed planner test explicitly expects no restore entry; applyCleanupPlan therefore neither restores it nor reports it. Modified unpreserved files only produce console.warn output, with no mechanism shown for adding the warning to the batch CheckRun output required by the goal.

The snapshot, planner, and cleanup abstractions do not compose coherently for budget-exceeded files: snapshotWorkspace records metadata-only ignored entries, planCheckSideEffectCleanup drops deleted metadata-only entries, and applyCleanupPlan can warn only about paths that reach toRestore. The design therefore has no end-to-end representation or reporting path for one of the corruption cases it intentionally introduces through preservation budgeting.

These are delivered-code defects and unfulfilled requirements, not missing process evidence.

The design bounds ignored-file reads and propagates unrestored-path warnings, but aggregate-budget selection is performed inside 64 concurrent stat workers using shared totalPreservedBytes. Completion order can differ between the before and after snapshots, so an untouched boundary file may receive a content hash in one snapshot and a stat hash in the other. The planner then treats it as modified and may rewrite it or emit a false corruption warning, violating the explicit requirement that untouched ignored files not be rewritten.
